1.title: Designing Applications with Foundation Models
1.text: Welcome to Module seven: Designing Applications with Foundation Models. This module opens Domain three, and covers task statement three point one. You will learn how to choose a model, how its settings change the answers, how to bring in your own data with Retrieval Augmented Generation, what it costs to customize a model, and what an A I agent does. The exam gives you a design need and asks you to name the right choice.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Identify the criteria for choosing a foundation model, including prompt caching. Describe how inference parameters, such as temperature, change responses. Define R A G, name its business uses and the vector stores on A W S. Explain the cost trade-offs of the customization approaches. And define the role of A I agents and their business uses.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Designs the Booking Assistant
1.text: At Cedar and Salt Travel, the team will build a booking assistant. It must answer policy questions and plan trips. The engineers ask which model to use, which settings to choose, and how to use the company's own documents. They also ask where to store embeddings, whether to tune the model, and whether it can act for guests. Your job is to make the design choices that the exam names.

1.title: Criteria for Choosing a Foundation Model
1.text: Start with the criteria for choosing a model. Cost: the price per input and output token. Modality: text, image, audio or video, in and out. Latency: how fast the answer must arrive. Multi-lingual: does it work well in your guests' languages? Model size and model complexity: bigger is more capable but costs more, so ask whether a simpler model is enough. Customization: can you tune or distill it? Input and output length: do your documents fit the context window? And prompt caching: is it supported? Exam tip: match the need to the criterion. Speed is latency, many languages is multi-lingual, and long documents is input length.

1.title: Reading the Criteria
1.text: Here is how to read those criteria. A larger model is usually slower and costlier, so start with the smallest one that meets the quality bar. The context window caps how much can go in, and the output length caps the answer; more tokens mean more cost and more time. For languages, test quality in each language you serve, not only English. Some models can be fine-tuned or distilled, so check that before you choose. And a task that reads photos needs a multi-modal model. Exam tip: if documents are too long for the model, pick a longer context window, or retrieve only the relevant parts.

1.title: Prompt Caching
1.text: Prompt caching is an optional feature that reduces response latency and input token cost. It helps when you have long, repeated context, such as a chat where users upload a document and ask many questions about it. Implicit caching is automatic and best effort. Explicit caching uses cache checkpoints that you set. Put static content first and changing content last, so the beginning of the prompt can match. The cache has a time to live, often five minutes, which resets on each hit. A hit is not guaranteed, and batch inference does not support it. As of five November twenty twenty-six, support, minimum sizes and time to live vary by model, so check the current documentation. Exam tip: the same long context sent again and again means prompt caching.

1.title: Inference Parameters: Temperature, Top K and Top P
1.text: Inference parameters change how the model picks the next token. Temperature: a lower value makes answers more predictable, because likelier tokens win; a higher value makes them more varied. Top K limits the choice to a fixed number of the most likely candidates. Top P limits it to a share of the total probability, so the pool size varies. For example, say the candidates are horses at zero point seven, zebras at zero point two, and unicorns at zero point one. Top K of two keeps horses and zebras. Top P of zero point seven keeps only horses. Exam tip: factual and consistent means a low temperature; creative and varied means a high temperature.

1.title: Length Parameters and Stop Sequences
1.text: Other settings control length. Response length sets the maximum, or minimum, number of tokens to return. A limit that is too low cuts the answer off; a higher one allows long answers but costs more and takes longer. A stop sequence is text that stops generation as soon as the model writes it. Penalties discourage repeated or frequent tokens, or very long responses. On the input side, the prompt, the documents and the history must fit the context window. And under on-demand pricing, you pay for tokens in and tokens out. Exam tip: an answer that stops mid-sentence means you should raise the maximum response length.

1.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
1.text: Now Retrieval Augmented Generation, or R A G. R A G draws information from your own data store to augment what the model answers. The picture shows the steps. The question becomes an embedding. The system searches a vector store that was filled in advance from your documents. The best chunks are added to the prompt. Then the foundation model writes the answer. There is no retraining, answers stay current, and they can cite sources. Grounding in real documents also helps reduce hallucinations. Exam tip: if the need is to use our own, current documents without retraining, the answer is R A G.

1.title: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
1.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is managed R A G. It is an out-of-the-box solution that automates the pipeline. At ingestion, you connect a data source, such as documents in Amazon S three. The text is split into chunks, turned into embeddings and stored in a vector index. At question time, the question is embedded, the index is searched, the chunks are added to the prompt, and the model generates the answer. It can return direct quotations from the sources, or a natural response. You do not need to keep training the model on your private data. Quick create can build a vector store for you. Exam tip: managed R A G on A W S is Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

1.title: Business Applications of RAG
1.text: R A G has many business uses. Customer support: a chat that answers from policy and help pages. Internal knowledge search: staff ask about procedures and policies. Document question answering: answers from contracts and reports, with citations. Personalization: recommendations that use customer and product data. And research: finding and summarizing facts across many long documents. Exam tip: when private or fast-changing knowledge sits behind an answer, think R A G.

1.title: Vector Databases: AWS Services That Store Embeddings
1.text: Embeddings need a vector store, and A W S offers several. Amazon OpenSearch Service gives distributed search and analytics, with full-text plus vector search. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon R D S for PostgreSQL add the p g vector extension to a relational database. Amazon Neptune Analytics offers graph analytics with vector search, for Graph R A G. Amazon Document D B is a document database with native vector search. Amazon Memory D B is in-memory, for ultra-low latency. And Amazon S three Vectors is low-cost storage for infrequent queries. ElastiCache for Valkey also offers vector search, and Dynamo D B data can be searched by vector through a zero-E T L link to OpenSearch Service. Exam tip: know the four named in the guide: OpenSearch Service, Aurora, Neptune and R D S for PostgreSQL.

1.title: Choosing a Vector Store
1.text: How do you choose? If you need S Q L and vector queries in one database, choose Aurora PostgreSQL with p g vector. For high-throughput search with full-text, choose OpenSearch Service. For relationships between entities, choose Neptune Analytics. For billions of vectors at the lowest cost, choose S three Vectors. For a MongoDB-compatible application, choose Document D B. And if you want no infrastructure to manage, choose Knowledge Bases with quick create. All of these work with I A M, K M S encryption and V P C support, and the embeddings model's dimensions must match the vector index. Exam tip: existing PostgreSQL means p g vector; graph relationships means Neptune; full-text plus vector means OpenSearch.

2.title: Customizing a Model: The Cost Ladder
2.text: Now the cost trade-offs of customizing. The picture is a ladder from cheapest to most costly. Prompts and in-context learning need no training; you pay for the tokens in longer prompts. R A G needs no training either, but adds embeddings, a vector store and retrieval, plus longer prompts. Fine-tuning or continued pre-training is billed on tokens processed times epochs, plus monthly model storage. Distillation costs a training run once, and then you run a smaller, faster, cheaper model. Pre-training a model is typically the highest in resources and cost. Exam tip: cheapest first. Prompts, then R A G, then tuning, then building a model.

2.title: Which Approach, and When?
2.text: Which approach fits which situation? If the task works but the wording needs help, use prompt engineering, with examples in the prompt. If answers need current or private facts, use R A G. For a specific task with labeled data, use fine-tuning. For domain-specific language, such as legal terms, use continued pre-training or fine-tuning. If a big model is too slow or costly for a narrow task, distill it into a smaller one. And if no model fits and you hold vast data, you could pre-train a custom model. The Well-Architected Generative A I Lens says to start with the least resource-intensive option and evaluate after each step. Exam tip: do not customize first. Prompts and R A G come before tuning.

2.title: AI Agents
2.text: Now A I agents. An agent uses a foundation model to understand a request and break it into smaller steps. It calls A P I s of company systems, asks the user for missing details, and queries knowledge bases to add information. Agents for Amazon Bedrock orchestrate models, data sources, applications and conversations. That service has a new name: it is now Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic. For new agents, A W S points to the Strands Agents S D K and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. As of five November twenty twenty-six, new sign-ups for Agents Classic are closed, and existing users continue. Exam tip: a multi-step task that calls A P I s is an agent, and the exam may still say Agents for Amazon Bedrock.

2.title: Business Applications of AI Agents
2.text: Agents have clear business uses. Insurance claims: the agent gathers details, checks the policy and files the claim. Travel reservations: the agent finds options, asks for missing details and books through an A P I. Customer service: it answers questions and takes actions, such as changing a booking. Task automation: it repeats routine steps across company systems. The key difference from R A G is that R A G answers from documents, while an agent also acts. Exam tip: answering from documents is R A G; completing a multi-step task through A P I s is an agent.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Designing with FMs
2.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Which criterion: cost, modality, latency, languages, size, complexity, customization, length or caching. Which parameter: temperature, Top K, Top P, response length or a stop sequence. Which approach: prompts first, R A G for current data, and fine-tuning for a specific task. Which store: OpenSearch Service, Aurora, R D S for PostgreSQL, Neptune and others. And which feature: Knowledge Bases for managed R A G, and agents for multi-step tasks. Exam tip: name the need first, then the criterion, setting, approach or service.

2.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Assistant
2.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and name the answer. Answers in about a second on a tight budget: a smaller model, checked for latency and price per token. Guests write in several languages: a multi-lingual model, tested in each. The same long policy goes with every question: prompt caching. Policy answers must be consistent: a low temperature. Policies change every week: R A G with Knowledge Bases. Link hotels, partners and trips by relationships: Neptune Analytics, for Graph R A G. And find options, ask for details and book a trip: an agent. Pause the video if you want more time.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Model criteria: cost, modality, latency, languages, size, complexity, customization, length and prompt caching. Parameters: a low temperature gives steady answers, Top K and Top P limit candidates, and length settings cap the output. R A G adds your own, current data without retraining, and Knowledge Bases is managed R A G. Vector stores include OpenSearch Service, Aurora, R D S for PostgreSQL, Neptune and more. Customization cost rises from prompts, to R A G, to tuning or distillation, to pre-training. And agents break tasks into steps and call A P I s.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A developer lowers the temperature of a foundation model from a high value to a low value. What is the most likely effect? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: responses become more consistent and predictable. A lower temperature steepens the probability distribution, so the model picks higher-probability tokens. A higher temperature gives more varied responses, and length is set with response length parameters.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Cedar and Salt's assistant sends the same long policy document with every guest question, and cost and latency are high. Which feature helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: prompt caching for the repeated policy text. Prompt caching reuses a repeated prompt prefix, which reduces latency and input token cost. Temperature, Top K and stop sequences do not change how a repeated prompt is processed or billed.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two are criteria for choosing a foundation model for an application? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Latency, price per token and input and output length are selection criteria, together with modality, languages, size, complexity, customization and prompt caching. Branding, staffing and office location do not describe the model.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Cedar and Salt's cancellation policy changes every week, and the assistant must use the latest text without retraining. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: use R A G with a knowledge base synced to the policy files. R A G retrieves current documents at question time, so updating the data source is enough. Pre-training and fine-tuning cost time and money every time, and temperature adds no facts.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Cedar and Salt wants answers that follow relationships between hotels, partners and trips, using vector search with graph traversal. Which service fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Amazon Neptune Analytics, for Graph R A G with vector search. It combines vector search with graph traversals and algorithms. S three Vectors suits cheap, infrequent retrieval, Memory D B suits ultra-low latency, and Document D B suits MongoDB-compatible applications.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which approach to improving a model's answers usually costs the least and should be tried first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: prompt engineering, with examples in the prompt. The Well-Architected Generative A I Lens says to start with the least resource-intensive option, then evaluate R A G, and customize only if needed. Building a custom model is typically the highest in resources and cost.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two statements describe what an A I agent does? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. An agent uses a foundation model to understand a request, break it into steps, take actions through A P I calls, and query data sources or knowledge bases. It still needs a model, it does not store weights, and it cannot guarantee correctness.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: B. Question two: A. Question three: B and D. Question four: D. Question five: B. Question six: C. Question seven: A and E. That completes Module seven. Next, Module eight covers prompt engineering: techniques, best practices, risks, and prompt management in Amazon Bedrock.
